t: Machiavelli wrote for new rulers rather than hereditary ones, and set aside the classical tradition's concern with ideal regimes in favour of the effectual truth of how men live.
He wrote it in 1513, a few months after the Medici regime had arrested, tortured and banished him, and meant it for the Medici; it was printed only in 1532, five years after his death.
Its advice on cruelty, deceit and the keeping of one's word shocked contemporaries, put it on the Index in 1559, and left a lasting mark on the words Machiavellian and politics.
dyk: After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo, his extensive written comments on The Prince were found in the emperor's coach and taken by the Prussian military.
ev: Machiavelli writes a version of the treatise, under the Latin title De Principatibus
Giuliano di Lorenzo de' Medici, for whom the book was first intended, dies
The Prince is printed, five years after Machiavelli's death, with the permission of Pope Clement VII
Paul IV places The Prince and the Discourses on Livy on the Index, nearly stopping their publication in Catholic areas except France
Innocent Gentillet publishes his Discourse against Machiavelli in Geneva
Frederick the Great's Anti-Machiavel is published, written under the guidance of Voltaire

f.made: Niccolò Machiavelli, Italian diplomat and political philosopher, writing in 1513 after the Medici regained Florence; dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici
f.form: A short political treatise in the style of the mirrors for princes, in 26 chapters after a dedicatory letter; original Latin title De Principatibus, later Il Principe
f.where: Read in printed editions and translations; no manuscript in Machiavelli's own handwriting survives
f.known: The advice that it is safer to be feared than loved; the lion and the fox; virtù and fortuna; the case against mercenaries; the praise of Cesare Borgia; the word Machiavellian
